title: Hume and cause and effect
examples: What exactly does Hume mean when he talks about habit?
Can you explain the difference between correlation and causation?
How does this relate to science today?

explain.say: Hume suggests we do not actually see necessary connection.

items: But we do not see the link

explain.say: We only observe that one thing follows another time.
This expectation forms a psychological habit in our minds.
The problem of induction questions how we justify future predictions.
For example, the sun has risen every single day we recall.
In daily life, we assume the laws of nature remain constant.

faq.q: What is the difference between correlation and causation?
faq.a: Correlation means two things happen together, but causation means one thing directly makes the other happen. You might hear people say that ice cream sales and sunburns are correlated, but neither causes the other; the heat causes both.
asks: What is the relationship between these two concepts?

faq.q: If we cannot prove necessity, how does science work?
faq.a: Science works by building the best models based on repeated evidence, even if the underlying necessity remains a philosophical mystery. It relies on the best available predictive power.
asks: What is the basis of scientific prediction?

faq.q: Is Hume suggesting we should stop making predictions?
faq.a: No, he is pointing out the logical gap in our justification for predictions. He suggests we are more reliant on habit than pure logic for these beliefs.
asks: What is Hume's stance on prediction?

faq.q: Does this apply to human behaviour too?
faq.a: Yes, we often predict people's actions based on past behaviour, which is an inductive leap that Hume questioned. We assume people will act similarly tomorrow.
asks: Can we use this for psychology?

faq.q: What is the role of psychology in this problem?
faq.a: Hume argued that the expectation itself is a psychological habit, not a matter of pure reason. Our minds are trained to expect patterns.

facts: Hume argued that we never perceive the necessary connection between cause and effect.
The problem of induction questions the justification for drawing general conclusions from specific instances.
Our expectation of cause and effect is described by Hume as a psychological habit.
Correlation simply means two variables tend to change together.

quiz.say: If you see a glass fall and then it break, what does Hume say you actually observe?
quiz.show: A falling glass, then a broken glass
quiz.why: He argues that the connection itself is not visible to us.

wrong.1: This assumes we can see the invisible link.
wrong.2: This suggests the law is an observable thing.
wrong.3: Deduction requires premises that guarantee the conclusion.

quiz.say: Which concept describes the belief that the sun will rise tomorrow because it always has?
quiz.why: Induction is the process of generalizing from past observations to future cases.

wrong.0: Deduction moves from general rules to specific cases.
wrong.1: Correlation only describes a relationship, not the predictive leap.
wrong.2: Necessity is what we assume, not the process itself.

quiz.say: If two things are correlated, what does that mean?
quiz.why: It means they tend to occur or change at the same time.

wrong.0: Correlation does not mean the variables are the same thing.
wrong.1: The link might be purely coincidental, not logical.
wrong.3: This jumps to causation, which is not guaranteed by correlation.
